library(rvest)
library(tidyverse)
library(tidyr)
library(openxlsx)
library(readxl)

# Read the EudraCT codes from the file (reads first column from first sheet)
eudract_codes <- read_excel("EUCTR_rvest_data/EUCTR_output.xlsx", sheet = 1, col_names = FALSE, skip = 1)[[1]]

# Remove duplicates
eudract_codes <- unique(eudract_codes)

# Define the variables to scrape
variables <- c("Reporting group title",
               "Reporting group description")

# Create an empty dataframe to store the cumulative data
cumulative_group_description <- data.frame(matrix(ncol = length(variables) + 1, nrow = 0))
colnames(cumulative_group_description) <- c("EudraCT_code", variables)

# Loop through each EudraCT code
for (eudract_code in eudract_codes) {
  
  # Construct the URL using the EudraCT code
  url <- paste0("https://www.clinicaltrialsregister.eu/ctr-search/trial/", eudract_code, "/results")
  
  # Read the HTML content of the trial results page
  page <- read_html(url)
  
  # Extract the data for each variable
  data_list <- lapply(variables, function(var) {
    values <- page %>% 
      html_nodes(paste0("td.labelColumn:contains('", var, "') + td.valueColumn")) %>%
      html_text(trim = T)
    return(values)
  })
  
  # Combine the data into a list with the EudraCT code and the variable values
  data_list <- c(list(eudract_code), data_list)
  
  # Find the max number of rows needed for this EudraCT code
  num_rows <- max(sapply(data_list, length))
  
  # Create a temporary data frame to store the extracted data
  temp_df <- data.frame(matrix(ncol = length(variables) + 1, nrow = num_rows))
  colnames(temp_df) <- c("EudraCT_code", variables)
  
  # Populate the temporary data frame with the extracted data
  for (i in 1:length(data_list)) {
    temp_df[[i]] <- rep(data_list[[i]], length.out = num_rows)
  }
  
  # Append the temporary data frame to the cumulative data frame
  cumulative_group_description <- rbind(cumulative_group_description, temp_df)
}

# Export the cumulative data to a new Excel file
write.xlsx(cumulative_group_description, "EUCTR_rvest_data/Group_Descriptions.xlsx", rowNames = FALSE)

What are the following GPT parameters:


Top-p (nucleus sampling)
Temperature

turns.speaker: model_b
turns.content:
Top-p (nucleus sampling) and Temperature are two parameters used to control the output diversity and quality during text generation from a language model like GPT (Generative Pre-trained Transformer).

1. Top-p (nucleus sampling): This is a sampling strategy where the model selects the next token in a generated sequence from a narrowed down distribution rather than from the full distribution of potential tokens. The probability distribution is truncated, considering only the tokens with the highest probability values that sum up to p. For example, if we set the top-p parameter to 0.9, the model would only consider the tokens with the highest probability that together account for 90% of the total probability mass. This selective process filters out less probable tokens, which reduces the chances of generating less meaningful text. Top-p (nucleus sampling) introduces diversity into the generated text without sacrificing quality.

2. Temperature: This parameter controls the randomness in the output text. It scales the probability distribution of the tokens. A higher temperature (e.g., 1.0 or greater) yields more random outputs, resulting in a more diverse set of generated sequences. Conversely, a lower temperature (e.g., 0.1 or less) leads to more focused sampling, which means the generated text is more deterministic and influenced by the highest probability tokens. In other words, lower temperature values make the model generate more conservative text, while higher temperature values make it more creative but potentially less coherent.

Both parameters are critical when fine-tuning text generation models like GPT, and they can be adjusted depending on the use case and desired level of text diversity and quality.

When using GPT for coding assistance, you would want the generated code to be accurate, coherent, and contextually relevant. Therefore, it is important to balance the generation parameters properly. Here are some suggestions for adjusting Top-p (nucleus sampling) and Temperature:

1. Top-p (nucleus sampling): Since coding assistance requires more precise token generation, it is better to set the Top-p value relatively high, such as around 0.8 to 0.95. This ensures that the selected tokens come from the more probable part of the distribution, making the generated code more likely to be correct and relevant to the context.

2. Temperature: For coding assistance, you want the generated code to be focused and coherent. A low to moderate temperature value, such as 0.5 to 0.7, would be a good starting point. Lower temperature values lead to more deterministic outputs, while slightly higher values still allow for some diversity in generated code. If the generated code is too repetitive or bland, you can slightly increase the temperature to introduce more variability.

Please note that the optimal values for these parameters can depend on the specific model you're using and the context of your task. Thus, it is recommended to experiment with different values and observe the quality of the generated code. You can perform several iterations with different parameter values and choose the settings that yield the best results for your coding assistance task.
